title: K-th Smallest Prime Fraction
statement:
The array `arr` is in strictly increasing order: its first entry is `1` and every later entry is a prime, so no value repeats. Each pair of indices `i < j` produces the fraction `arr[i] / arr[j]`. Imagine listing all of these fractions from smallest to largest; return the one in position `k` (counting from 1) as a two-element array `[arr[i], arr[j]]`, numerator first.

Because the values are 1 and distinct primes, no two of these fractions are equal, so the answer is always unique.
constraints: arr[i] is a prime number for every i > 0
arr is strictly increasing, so all values are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Listing all `n(n-1)/2` fractions and sorting them works but costs O(n² log n). Notice that for a fixed denominator `arr[j]` the fractions `arr[0]/arr[j] < arr[1]/arr[j] < ... < arr[j-1]/arr[j]` already form a sorted chain. The task becomes "merge `n - 1` sorted chains and stop at the k-th item", which a min-heap does by always holding the smallest unused fraction of every chain.

## Approach

1. Store each fraction as an index pair `[i, j]`. Compare two pairs with cross multiplication (`arr[a0] * arr[b1] < arr[b0] * arr[a1]`), which avoids floating-point error.
2. Push the head of every chain, `[0, j]` for each `j` from 1 to `n - 1`.
3. Pop the smallest fraction `k - 1` times. After popping `[i, j]`, push the next fraction of the same chain, `[i + 1, j]`, if `i + 1 < j`.
4. The heap's top is now the k-th smallest; return `[arr[i], arr[j]]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [1, 2, 3, 5]`, `k = 3`. The heap starts with `1/2`, `1/3`, `1/5`.
- `count = 1`: pop `1/5` (`[0, 3]`), push `2/5` (`[1, 3]`). Heap: `1/2`, `1/3`, `2/5`.
- `count = 2`: pop `1/3` (`[0, 2]`), push `2/3` (`[1, 2]`). Heap: `1/2`, `2/5`, `2/3`.
- The loop ends; the top is `2/5`, so the answer is `[2, 5]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O((n + k) log n): the heap never holds more than `n - 1` entries and each push or pop costs O(log n).
- Space: O(n) for the heap.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing `arr[i] / arr[j]` as floating-point numbers is risky; the cross products are at most about 9 * 10^8 and compare exactly.
- Pop only `k - 1` times and then read the top; popping `k` times and reading the top returns the (k+1)-th fraction.
- Only push `[i + 1, j]` while `i + 1 < j`: a numerator index must stay below its denominator index.
- Return the values `arr[i]` and `arr[j]`, not the indices.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `heap` | min-heap of index pairs `[i, j]`, ordered by `arr[i] / arr[j]` |
| `less` | true when the first pair's fraction is smaller than the second's |
| `push`, `pop` | insert into and remove the smallest entry from the heap |
| `child`, `parent`, `left`, `right`, `smallest` | positions used while sifting inside the heap |
| `count` | how many fractions have been popped so far, plus one |
| `i`, `j` | numerator and denominator indices of a fraction |
